title: Prompt-engineering patterns
summary: Reusable patterns - roles, few-shot, structured output and chaining - that make a language model's answers reliable enough to ship.
objectives: Write a clear instruction with a role, task, and constraints
Use a system prompt to set persistent behaviour
Force machine-readable answers with structured output
Split hard problems into a chain of smaller prompts
Call the Claude Messages API in Python with a model id and max_tokens
Evaluate a prompt and iterate instead of guessing

quiz.q: What is the role of a system prompt?
options: It sets persistent behaviour and persona for the whole conversation
It is the user's first question
It limits how many tokens you are billed for
quiz.why: The system prompt frames who the model is and how it should behave across every turn, separate from the per-message user content.

options: Asking the same question several times
Giving a few worked input-output examples so the model copies the pattern
Using fewer tokens to save money
Calling the model with a tiny max_tokens
quiz.why: Few-shot means including a handful of example pairs in the prompt so the model infers the format and style you want.

quiz.q: Why ask the model for JSON output instead of free text?
options: JSON can be parsed reliably by your code without fragile string-matching
The model thinks harder in JSON
It is the only format the API accepts
quiz.why: Structured output (e.g. JSON) lets your program read fields directly, instead of guessing meaning from prose that varies each run.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is prompt chaining and when would you use it?
quiz.answer: Splitting a task into a sequence of prompts where each step's output feeds the next; use it when one prompt is doing too much or accuracy drops.
quiz.why: Chaining keeps each step simple and checkable - extract, then summarise, then format - which is far more reliable than one giant prompt.

quiz.q: Name one reason you should keep your API key in an environment variable, not in your code.
quiz.answer: So the secret is never committed to Git or shared, keeping it out of your portfolio repo and version history.
quiz.why: Hard-coded keys leak when you push to GitHub; reading ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment keeps the secret private.

quiz.q: What does the temperature-free, deterministic-leaning approach of giving explicit constraints buy you?
options: More predictable, on-spec answers that are easier to test
quiz.why: Explicit constraints (length, format, what to avoid) narrow the model's choices, so outputs vary less and are easier to evaluate.

body_markdown:
## Why prompt patterns?

A **prompt** is the text you send to a language model. Beginners type a question and hope. Engineers use **patterns** - reusable shapes that turn a vague request into a reliable, testable instruction. For your portfolio projects this is the difference between a demo that works once and a feature that works every time.

Think of it like a function signature: a good prompt states the **role**, the **task**, the **inputs**, and the **constraints** on the output.

## Pattern 1: role, task, constraints

Don't just say *"summarise this"*. Say who the model is, what to do, and what the answer must look like.

```text
You are a careful financial analyst.
Summarise the email below in exactly 3 bullet points.
Do not invent numbers. If a figure is missing, write "not stated".
```

The role sets tone, the task is the verb, and the constraints (3 bullets, no invented numbers) make the output predictable - and therefore testable.

## Pattern 2: system prompt + few-shot

The **system prompt** sets persistent behaviour for the whole conversation. **Few-shot** prompting adds a few worked examples so the model copies the pattern. Here is a minimal Claude Messages API call in Python:

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You label support tickets. Reply with one word: billing, bug, or other.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "My card was charged twice."},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "billing"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "The app crashes on login."},
    ],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)  # -> bug
```

The earlier user/assistant pair is the single example that teaches the format.

## Pattern 3: structured output

When your code needs to *read* the answer, ask for JSON and parse it - never string-match prose.

```python
import json
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
        'Extract name and city as JSON keys "name" and "city": '
        '"Ada Lovelace lives in London."'}],
)
data = json.loads(msg.content[0].text)
print(data["city"])  # -> London
```

## Pattern 4: prompt chaining

If one prompt is doing too much, break it into steps where each output feeds the next: **extract -> summarise -> format**. Each step is simple, so each step is easy to check and fix. This is the single biggest reliability win in real projects.

## Your task

Take one feature in your portfolio project and rewrite its prompt using **role, task, constraints** plus one **few-shot example**. Keep your key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

bullets: A prompt is the text you send the model.
Beginners type a question and hope.

An engineer uses patterns - reusable shapes that make the answer predictable. Think of a prompt like a function signature: you state the role, the task, the inputs, and the constraints on the output. slides.title: Role, task, constraints
bullets: State who the model is.
State the task as a clear verb.
Constrain the output: length, format, what to avoid.
Constraints make outputs testable.
slides.code:
You are a careful analyst.
Summarise the email in exactly
3 bullet points.
Do not invent numbers.
slides.narration: The first pattern is role, task, constraints. Don't just say summarise this. Say who the model is - a careful analyst. Say the task as a verb - summarise. Then constrain the output: exactly three bullets, and do not invent numbers. Those constraints are the important part, because they make the answer predictable, and a predictable answer is one you can actually test.

slides.title: The system prompt
bullets: Sets persistent behaviour for the whole chat.
Separate from the per-message user content.
Use it for persona, rules, and output format.
It is not the user's question.
slides.code:
system="You label tickets.
Reply with one word:
billing, bug, or other."
slides.narration: The system prompt sets persistent behaviour for the entire conversation - the persona and the rules that apply on every turn. It's separate from the user messages, which carry the actual questions. Here the system prompt tells the model it labels support tickets and must reply with a single word. Set the behaviour once in the system prompt, and you don't have to repeat it in every message.

slides.title: Few-shot examples
bullets: Show a few input-output examples.
The model copies the pattern.
Great for format and labelling tasks.
Often beats a longer instruction.
slides.narration: Few-shot prompting means giving the model a few worked examples so it copies the pattern. Here we show one user message paired with the correct one-word answer, billing, and then a new question. The model infers the format from that example and replies bug. For format-heavy and labelling tasks, a couple of good examples often work better than a long paragraph of instructions.

slides.title: Calling the API
bullets: Import the Anthropic client.
Pass a model id and max_tokens.
Keep your key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
Read the text from msg.content.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
  model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
  max_tokens=1024,
  messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Here's the actual A P I call in Python. You import the Anthropic client, which reads your key from the environment variable ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY - never hard-code it. Then you call messages dot create with a model id, a max tokens limit, and your list of messages. The reply comes back in msg dot content, and you read the text from the first block. That's the whole shape of every Claude request.

slides.title: Structured output
bullets: Ask for JSON when your code must read the answer.
Parse it - never string-match prose.
Name the exact keys you want.
Predictable fields, easy to test.
slides.code:
content='Extract as JSON keys
"name" and "city": Ada lives
in London.'
data = json.loads(msg.content[0].text)
print(data["city"])  # London
slides.narration: When your program needs to read the answer, ask for structured output - usually Jason - and parse it. Name the exact keys you want, here name and city. Then your code calls json dot loads and reads the city field directly. This is far more reliable than trying to pull meaning out of free-form prose that looks slightly different on every run. Predictable fields mean code you can actually trust.

slides.title: Prompt chaining
bullets: Split a hard task into a sequence of prompts.
Each step's output feeds the next.
Extract, then summarise, then format.
Each step is simple and checkable.
slides.code:
step1 = extract(raw_text)
step2 = summarise(step1)
final = format_json(step2)
slides.narration: When one prompt is trying to do too much and accuracy drops, chain it. Split the task into a sequence: first extract the facts, then summarise them, then format the result. Each step's output feeds into the next. Because every step is small and focused, it's easy to check and easy to fix when something goes wrong. Chaining is the single biggest reliability win in real projects.

slides.title: Iterate, don't guess
bullets: Test the prompt on a few real inputs.
Tighten the constraint that failed.
Keep examples that fix mistakes.
Treat the prompt like code you debug.
slides.narration: A prompt is not something you write once and walk away from. Run it on a handful of real inputs, see where it fails, and tighten the specific constraint that broke. If a few-shot example fixes a recurring mistake, keep it. Treat your prompt like code: you write it, you test it, you debug it, and you improve it. That habit is what separates a hobby script from a portfolio-ready feature.
